title: Epstein-Barr virus (mono)
what: This blood test looks for antibodies to the Epstein-Barr virus. It helps show whether you have mono now or had it before.
why: For a long fever, a very sore throat, swollen glands in the neck, and weakness. It is common in children and teenagers.
duration: the blood draw takes a few minutes; results usually come in 1 to 3 days
tell_doctor: How many days the fever has lasted
What antibiotics or other medicines you took
If there is pain on the left side of the belly under the ribs

prepare.title: Food
prepare.text: You usually do not need to fast strictly, but it is better to come 3 to 4 hours after a light, non-fatty meal. Check with the lab.

prepare.title: Medicines
prepare.text: Do not stop anything on your own. Tell your doctor what you take. They will decide if anything needs to change before the test.

prepare.title: Your child
prepare.text: If a child is being tested, tell them there will be a quick prick. Bring water and a snack for afterward.

prepare.title: Clothing
prepare.text: A sleeve you can easily roll up above the elbow.

bring: Your referral or list of tests
Your complete blood count, if you already had one
steps: You sit down and rest your arm on the armrest
A band is tied above your elbow, and you are asked to clench your fist a few times
The skin is wiped with antiseptic
A quick prick. Blood fills the tubes in a few seconds
The needle comes out, and a cotton pad is pressed on the spot
feel: A quick prick, like a pinch
Sometimes slight dizziness. Tell the nurse, and they will help you lie down
A child may get scared. Stay close and hold their hand
after: Press the cotton pad for 3 to 5 minutes
Until your doctor says otherwise: no sports or rough play. Mono makes the spleen bigger
Your doctor will explain the result. Usually several types of antibodies are checked
red_flags: Sudden pain on the left side of the belly, weakness, or paleness: call emergency services
Trouble breathing or swallowing: call emergency services
Fever lasting more than a week: tell your doctor

faq.a: Mostly through saliva: kissing, shared cups, and toys. Most people get it in childhood.
With mono, the spleen is enlarged and can be injured by a hit. Your doctor will say when you can go back to sports.

reminders.text: Epstein-Barr virus test tomorrow. Better to skip fatty food in the morning.
